citations.quote:
Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim:
The exact objective is also the finite graph with maps $\Phi_n$, costs $K_n$, initial state $u(0)$ and terminal cost $\phi$: the intervals partition the integral. Differentiability of $K_n$ follows by differentiating its integral using the common-tube flow derivative and the uniform continuous derivative bounds. In particular the initial-state variational matrix $V$ on interval $n$ has $V(t_n)=I$, $V'=f_uV$, and
$$c_n^e=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}V(t)^T\ell_u(t)^T\,dt.$$
The pairing identity gives
$$p(t_n)=c_n^e(u(t_n),\theta)+A_n^e(u(t_n),\theta)^Tp(t_{n+1}).$$
Thus the exact-flow graph adjoint equals the continuous adjoint at every node. Its tangent and gradient are also those of the exact continuous objective.

Write $u_n=u(t_n)$ and $e_n=\|x_n-u_n\|$. For $d\ge1$, parameterize the admitted segment by $s\mapsto u_n+s(x_n-u_n)$, $0\le s\le1$. The chain rule and the derivative bound for $\Psi_n$ bound the derivative of its composition with this segment by $(1+Lh)\|x_n-u_n\|$; the vector mean value inequality [F1] therefore gives its endpoint Lipschitz bound with constant $1+Lh$. For $d=0$, the state difference and both endpoint values lie in the zero vector space, so the same bound is immediate. Consequently
$$e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+c_vh^{p+1}.$$
By [F3], $e_n\le Xh^p$.

The exact tangent and adjoint recurrences give
$$\|S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n\|+Mh,\qquad \|p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p(t_{n+1})\|+Mh.$$
Expanding these finite recurrences and using $(1+Lh)^k\le e^{LT}$ shows $\|S_n\|\le\overline S$ and $\|p(t_n)\|\le\overline P$. These bounds include $L=0$. For any one of the four derivative maps, comparison at numerical and exact nodes gives
$$\|F_n^h(x_n,\theta)-F_n^e(u_n,\theta)\|\le c_1h^{p+1}+Hh e_n\le Rh^{p+1}.$$

The actual differentiated numerical graph satisfies $S_{n+1}^h=A_n^h(x_n)S_n^h+B_n^h(x_n)$. Subtract the exact recurrence and split the matrix product using $A_n^h(S_n^h-S_n)+(A_n^h-A_n^e)S_n$. Hence
$$\|S_{n+1}^h-S_{n+1}\|\le(1+Lh)\|S_n^h-S_n\|+R(\overline S+1)h^{p+1}.$$
The initial derivative bound and [F3] yield $C_Sh^p$.

At the terminal node, the difference of adjoint seeds is at most $Dh^p$. Subtract the two backward recurrences, splitting $A_h^Tp_h-A_e^Tp_e=A_h^T(p_h-p_e)+(A_h-A_e)^Tp_e$. The Euclidean operator norm of a transpose equals that of the matrix. For every finite-dimensional Euclidean vector $v$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|v\|=\sup_{\|w\|\le1}|w^Tv|$: if $v\ne0$, equality is attained at $w=v/\|v\|$, while for $v=0$ both sides vanish, including in dimension zero. Applying this closed-unit-ball formula to both sides of the pairing gives the transpose identity in all finite dimensions. Therefore
$$\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le(1+Lh)\|p_{n+1}^h-p(t_{n+1})\|+R(\overline P+1)h^{p+1}.$$
Reverse the indices and apply [F3]. This gives $C_Ph^p$.

Apply the finite-graph gradient formula to both graphs:
$$\nabla J_h=D_\theta\phi_h(x_N)^T+(S_0^h)^Tp_0^h+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^h(x_n)+(B_n^h(x_n))^Tp_{n+1}^h\},$$
$$\nabla J=D_\theta\phi(u_N)^T+S_0^Tp(0)+\sum_{n<N}\{d_n^e(u_n)+(B_n^e(u_n))^Tp(t_{n+1})\}.$$
The terminal direct-derivative difference is at most $Dh^p$. The initial contribution is bounded by
$$\{c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P\}h^p,$$
since $h\le1$ implies $\|S_0^h\|\le M_0+c_{s0}$. Each running difference is bounded by
$$\{R+R\overline P+MC_P\}h^{p+1},$$
using $B_h^T(p_h-p)+(B_h-B_e)^Tp$. Summing $N$ terms and using $Nh=T$ proves the stated $C_G$ bound.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

For $r=e,h$, define
$$A_n^e=D_x\Phi_n,\quad B_n^e=D_\theta\Phi_n,\quad c_n^e=D_xK_n^T,\quad d_n^e=D_\theta K_n^T,$$
$$A_n^h=D_x\Psi_n,\quad B_n^h=D_\theta\Psi_n,\quad c_n^h=D_xL_n^T,\quad d_n^h=D_\theta L_n^T.$$
Suppose constants $c_v,c_1,L,M,H\ge0$ satisfy, at each admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|\Psi_n-\Phi_n\|\le c_vh^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^h-A_n^e\|,\ \|B_n^h-B_n^e\|,\ \|c_n^h-c_n^e\|,\ \|d_n^h-d_n^e\|\le c_1h^{p+1},$$
$$\|A_n^r\|\le1+Lh,\qquad \|B_n^r\|,\ \|c_n^r\|,\ \|d_n^r\|\le Mh.$$
Each of $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$ is Lipschitz in $x$, with constant at most $Hh$.

Let $S_0=D_\theta u(0,\theta)$ and $S_0^h=D_\theta x_0(\theta)$. Assume
$$\|x_0-u(0)\|\le c_0h^p,\qquad \|S_0^h-S_0\|\le c_{s0}h^p,\qquad \|S_0\|\le M_0.$$
The terminal costs are $C^1$. The exact columns $D_x\phi^T,D_\theta\phi^T$ have norm at most $M_\phi$ and are Lipschitz in $x$ with constant $H_\phi$; at the same admitted $(x,\theta)$,
$$\|D_x\phi_h^T-D_x\phi^T\|,\ \|D_\theta\phi_h^T-D_\theta\phi^T\|\le C_\phi h^p.$$
No terminal value-error hypothesis is needed for the gradient conclusion.

Let $S_n^h=D_\theta x_n$, and let $p_n^h$ be the exact discrete adjoint of this numerical graph. Let $S(t)=D_\theta u(t)$ and let $p(t)$ be the continuous adjoint with terminal value $D_x\phi(u(T),\theta)^T$. Define
$$E=e^{LT},\quad X=E(c_0+Tc_v),\quad \overline S=E(M_0+TM),\quad \overline P=E(M_\phi+TM),$$
$$R=c_1+HX,\quad C_S=E\{c_{s0}+TR(\overline S+1)\},\quad D=C_\phi+H_\phi X,$$
$$C_P=E\{D+TR(\overline P+1)\},$$
$$C_G=D+c_{s0}\overline P+(M_0+c_{s0})C_P+T\{R(1+\overline P)+MC_P\}.$$
Then
$$\max_n\|x_n-u(t_n)\|\le Xh^p,\qquad \max_n\|S_n^h-S(t_n)\|\le C_Sh^p,$$
$$\max_n\|p_n^h-p(t_n)\|\le C_Ph^p,\qquad \|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|\le C_Gh^p.$$
These conclusions assume local value and first-derivative consistency, rather than a global adjoint-error estimate. They require no representation by nonnegative quadrature weights.

derivations.claim:
Set $\xi=(x,\theta)$. The exact local solution has $V(t)=D_\xi u(t)$ because $V(t_n)=E$ and its displayed equation is the variational equation, with $D_\xi\theta=E_\theta$. Differentiating the cost integral gives $g(t)=D_\xi C(t)^T$. Thus at the local endpoint,
$$V^+=[D_x\Phi_n\ D_\theta\Phi_n],\qquad g^+=\begin{pmatrix}D_xK_n^T\\D_\theta K_n^T\end{pmatrix}.$$
The flow result and bounded continuous derivatives justify these differentiations uniformly.

Differentiate each actual stage, in its explicit order. If $V_i=D_\xi Y_i$, then
$$V_i=E+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}(f_{u,j}V_j+f_{\theta,j}E_\theta),$$
$$D_\xi\Psi_n=E+h\sum_i b_i(f_{u,i}V_i+f_{\theta,i}E_\theta),$$
$$D_\xi L_n^T=h\sum_i b_i(V_i^T\ell_{u,i}^T+E_\theta^T\ell_{\theta,i}^T).$$
These are exactly the $V$ and $g$ outputs obtained by applying the same RK tableau to the augmented system. Its $C$ output is $L_n$ and its $u$ output is $\Psi_n$. Consequently the assumed augmented local defect bounds $\Psi_n-\Phi_n$, $L_n-K_n$, and all four first-derivative differences by constants times $h^{p+1}$. Projection to a component does not increase the Euclidean norm; a matrix Frobenius bound also bounds its operator norm.

For a fixed finite tableau, the stage derivative recurrences in step 1.2 give uniform bounds on $D_xY_i,D_\theta Y_i$ by induction, using $h\le h_0$ and the bounded first derivatives of $f$. Here $D_xY_i=I+O(h)$ and $D_\theta Y_i=O(h)$. Substitution into the output derivatives gives
$$D_x\Psi_n=I+O(h),\quad D_\theta\Psi_n=O(h),\quad D_xL_n^T=O(h),\quad D_\theta L_n^T=O(h),$$
uniformly. In particular $\|D_x\Psi_n\|\le1+L_hh$ for a fixed constant $L_h$. The exact variational integral equation gives the same bounds for the exact maps, with $\|D_x\Phi_n\|\le e^{Kh}\le1+Ke^{Kh_0}h$. Enlarging the constants gives the common $L,M$ required by the preceding lemma.

The exact maps have the required second-derivative bounds of size $O(h)$. To justify differentiating their variational equations, apply the common-tube $C^1$ flow result to the first variational system: its field is $C^1$ since $f$ is $C^2$, its initial derivative seed is constant, and its variational components remain bounded by [F2]. For coordinate directions $a,b$ of $\xi$, put $W_{ab}=D_{\xi_a}D_{\xi_b}u$. Then
$$W_{ab}'=f_uW_{ab}+D^2_{(u,\theta)}f[(V_a,E_{\theta,a}),(V_b,E_{\theta,b})],\qquad W_{ab}(t_n)=0.$$
The forcing is uniformly bounded, so Grönwall on an interval of length $h$ gives $\|W_{ab}\|\le C h$. Differentiating the cost integral twice produces the integrand
$$D^2_{(u,\theta)}\ell[(V_a,E_{\theta,a}),(V_b,E_{\theta,b})]+\ell_uW_{ab},$$
which is uniformly bounded, and hence $D_\xi^2K_n=O(h)$. Thus $D_\xi^2\Phi_n=O(h)$ and $D_\xi^2K_n=O(h)$. Applying the one-dimensional mean value inequality along each admitted state segment gives Lipschitz constants $Hh$ for $A_n^e,B_n^e,c_n^e,d_n^e$.

Steps 1.2–3.1 establish precisely the local hypotheses of the preceding lemma. That lemma now proves the global state, actual graph-tangent, backward nodal-adjoint and gradient bounds. In particular the adjoint conclusion is derived; it is not inserted as an additional hypothesis.

There is also a direct augmented global-error interpretation. Along a full trajectory append $C'=\ell$ and the column $G'=S^T\ell_u^T+\ell_\theta^T$, with $C(0)=0,G(0)=0$ and $S'=f_uS+f_\theta$. Differentiating the actual stages shows that its numerical step is exactly
